review_notes: I read the whole file and the `selfAdjointPart` and `skewAdjointPart` definitions in Mathlib/Algebra/Star/Module.lean. I searched Mathlib for uses of `selfAdjointPartL` and `skewAdjointPartL` and found none outside this file. The `starL`/`starL'` simp lemmas (`toLinearEquiv_starL`, `symm_starL`, `symm_starL'`, `@[simps! apply]`) look fine, because each is a `rfl` lemma with a canonical left-hand side. I could not run Lean, so I don't know exactly what shape `simps!` generates for the two `*PartL` declarations. The finding therefore rests on the visible inconsistency between the two attributes, not on an observed simp failure. I also found no cycle or competing-rule problem.

findings.problem: The two parallel bundled maps have different simp interfaces. `selfAdjointPartL` is declared with `@[simps! -isSimp]`, so its generated `_apply` lemmas are not simp lemmas. `skewAdjointPartL` is declared with plain `@[simps!]`, so its lemmas are simp. The file gives no reason for the difference. The underlying linear maps `selfAdjointPart` and `skewAdjointPart` both use plain `@[simps]` in Mathlib/Algebra/Star/Module.lean, so both `_apply_coe` lemmas are simp there. Because of this, `simp` rewrites `skewAdjointPartL R A x` but leaves `selfAdjointPartL R A x` stuck. There is also no `@[simp]` lemma connecting the continuous map to its underlying linear map. `simps!` also fully unfolds the underlying definition, so the `skewAdjointPartL` simp lemma may expand the term to an explicit subtype structure instead of the canonical `skewAdjointPart R x`.
findings.proposed_change: Make the two declarations agree. Preferably give both the same `@[simps! -isSimp]`, or use plain `@[simps]` if the generated statement is the canonical `⇑(selfAdjointPartL R A) = ⇑(selfAdjointPart R)` form. Then add one explicit `@[simp]` lemma for each, stating `(selfAdjointPartL R A) x = selfAdjointPart R x` (and likewise for skew). This normalises both to the already-simp-tagged `selfAdjointPart_apply_coe` / `skewAdjointPart_apply_coe`. If `-isSimp` was added on purpose for `selfAdjointPartL`, apply the same fix to `skewAdjointPartL` and add a comment explaining it.
findings.benefit: `simp` then treats the self-adjoint and skew-adjoint continuous maps the same way and always reduces them to the linear-map form that has simp coverage. Users no longer meet one part that simplifies and one that does not, and neither unfolds into an implementation-level structure.

evidence.excerpt:
@[simps]
def selfAdjointPart : A →ₗ[R] selfAdjoint A where

@[simps]
def skewAdjointPart : A →ₗ[R] skewAdjoint A where
